And why? Iob hath sayde: I am ryghtuous, but GOD doth me wronge.
I muste nedes be a lyar, thoughe my cause be ryghte, and vyolently I am plaged where as I made no faut:
where is there such one as Iob, that drincketh vp scornefulnes lyke water?
which goeth in the company of wicked doars, & walketh with vngodly men?
For he sayeth: Thoughe a man be good, yet is he naughte before God.
Therfore herken vnto me, ye that haue vnderstandynge. Farre be it from God, that he shulde medle with wyckednesse: and farre be it from the almyghtye, that he shuld medle wyth vnryghtuous dealynge:
but he rewardeth the worckes of man, and causeth euerye man to fynde accordynge to hys wayes.
For sure it is, that God condemneth no man wrongouslye, and the iudgemente of the Almyghtye is not vnrightuous.
Who ruleth the earth in his stead? Or, whome hath he set to gouerne the whole worlde?
To whome hath he geuen hys herte, for to drawe hys spryte and breth vnto hym?
All flesh shall come together vnto naught, & all men shall turne agayne vnto earthe.
If thou nowe haue vnderstandynge, heare what I say, and herken to the voyce of my wordes.
Maye he be made whole, that loueth no ryghte? If thou were a verye innocente man, shuldest thou then be punysheth:
For he is euen the same, that knoweth the rebellyous kynges, and sayth to Princes:
Vngodly men are ye. He hath none respecte vnto the personnes of the lordlye, and regardeth not the ryche more then pore. For they be al the worcke of hys handes.
In the twynckelynge of an eye shal they be slayne: and at midnight, when the people and the tyrauntes rage, then shall they peryshe, and be taken awaye withoute handes.
And why? hys eyes loke vpon the wayes of man, and he seith all hys goynges.
There is no darcknes nor thicke shadow, that can hyde the wycked doers from hym.
For no man shalbe suffered to go into iudgemente wyth God.
Manye one, yea innumerable doth he punyshe, and setteth other in theyr steades.
For he knoweth theyr euyll and darcke worckes, therfore shall they be destroyed.
They that were in the steade of Sears, dealte lyke vngodly men.
Therfore turned they backe trayterously and vnfaythfully from hym, & wolde not receyue hys wayes.
In so muche that they haue caused the voyce of the poore to come vnto hym, and nowe he heareth the complaynte of suche as are in necessite.
If he delyuer and graunte pardon, who wil iudge or condemne? But yf he hyde away hys countenaunce, who wyll turne it aboute agayne, whether it be to the people or to anye man?
For the wyckednesse and synne of the people, he maketh an ypocryte to raygne ouer them.
For so muche then as I haue begonne to talke of GOD, I wyll not hyndre the.
If I haue gone a mysse, enfourme me: yf I haue done wronge, I wyl leaue of.
Wylte thou not geue a reasonable aunswere? Art thou afrayed of anye thynge, seynge thou begannest fyrste to speake, & not I?
For els the men of vnderstandyng & wysdome, that haue heard me, myght say: What canste thou speake?
As for Iob he hath nether spoken to the purpose nor wyselye.
O father, let Iob be well tryed, because he hath turned hym self to the wycked:
yea aboue hys synnes he hath blasphemed, whiche offence he hath done euen before vs, in that he stryueth against God with his wordes.
35: Thinkest thou it right that thou saiest: I am ryghteous before GOD?
Seynge, thou sayest so, howe doest thou knowe it? What thynge haste thou more excellente then I, that I am a synner?
Therfore wyll I geue answere vnto the and thy frendes:
loke vnto the heauen, and beholde it: consydre the cloudes, how they are hyer then thou.
If thou sinnest, what doest thou vnto hym? If thyne offences be manye, howe gettest thou his fauoure?
Yf thou be ryghteous what geuest thou hym? Or what receyueth he of thy handes?
Of such an vngodly personne as thou, and of the sonne of man that is ryghtuous as thou pretendeste to be:
there is a great crye & complaynt made by them that are oppressed with violence, yea euerye man complayneth vpon the cruell arme of tyrauntes.
For suche one neuer sayeth: Where is God that made me? & that shyneth vpon vs, that we myght prayse him in the nighte?
Whiche geueth vs more vnderstandyng then he doth the beastes of the earthe, and teacheth vs more then the foules of heauen.
If anye suche complayne, no man geueth answere, and that because of the wyckednesse of proude tyrauntes.
But yf a man call vpon God, doth not he heare him? Doth not the almyghtye accepte hys crye?
Whan thou speakest then, shulde not he pardon the, yf thou open thy selfe before hym, and put thy trust in hym?
Then vseth he no vyolence in his wrath nether hath the pleasure in curyous & depe inquisicions.
Therfore hath Iob opened hys mouthe but in vayne, and folyshlye hathe he made so many wordes.
36: Eliu proceaded forth in his talking & sayde:
Hold the styl a lytle, & I shal shew the, what I haue yet to speake on Godes behalfe.
I wil open vnto the yet more of myne vnderstandynge, and proue my maker righteous.
True are my wordes, & no lye: & the knowledge where with al I argue against the, is perfect.
Behold, God casteth not away the myghtye, for he hym selfe is myghtye in power and wysdome.
As for the vngodly, he preserueth them not, but helpeth the poore to their ryght.
He turneth not his eyes awaye from the ryghteous, he setteth vp kynges in theyr trone, and confyrmeth them, so that they alway sit there in.
But yf they be layed in preson & cheynes, or bounde with the bondes of pouertye:
then sheweth he them theyr worckes & dedes & the synnes where with they haue vsed cruell vyolence.
He wyth punyshynge and outtryng of them, roundeth them in the eares, warneth them to leaue of from theyr wyckednesse, and to amende.
If tney nowe wyll take hede, and be obedyente, they shall were oute theyr dayes in prosperyte, and theyr yeares in pleasure & ioye.
But yf they wyl not obeye, they shal go thorowe the swearde, and perysh or euer they be a warre.
As for suche as be fayned, dissemblers and ypocrytes, they heape vp wrath for them selues: for they call not vpon him, though they be hys presoners.
Thus theyr soule perysheth in folishnesse, and theyr lyfe wyth the condemned.
The poore delyuereth he oute of hys straytnesse, and comforteth suche as be in necessyte and trouble.
Euen so shall he kepe the (yf thou wylte be contente) from the bottomlesse pytte that is beneth: and yf thou wilt holde the quyete, he shall fyll thy table with plenteousnesse.
Neuerthelesse thou haste condemned the iudgemente of the vngodly, yea euen suche a iudgement and sentence shalt thou suffre.
For then shall not thy cause be stylled wyth crueltie, nor pacyfyed wyth manye gyftes.
Hath God ordeyned then, that the gloryous lyfe of the, & all suche myghtye men shuld not be put doune?
Prolonge not thou the tyme, tyl there come a nyght for the, to se other people in thy stead.
But bewarre that thou turne not a syde to wyckednesse and synne, whiche hyther to thou hast chosen more then mekenesse.
Behold God is of a myghtye hye power: Where is there soche a gyde and lawe geuer as he?
Who wyll reproue hym of his waye? who will saye vnto him: thou hast done wronge?
O consydre how greate and excellent his worckes be, whom all men loue and prayse:
yee wondre at hym, and yet they se hym but a farre of.
Beholde, so great is God, that he passeth oure knowledge, nether are we able to come to the experience of hys yeares.
He turneth the water to small droppes, he dryueth hys cloudes
to gether for to raygne, so that they poure downe and droppe vpon men.
He can sprede out the cloudes (a couerynge of hys tabernacle)
and cause hys lyght to shyne vpon them: and to couer the botome of the sea.
By these thinges gouerneth he hys people, and geueth them aboundaunce of meate.
In the turnynge of a hande he hydeth the lyght, & at hys commaundement it commeth agayne.
The rysinge vp therof sheweth he to his frendes and to the cattell.
37: At thys, my herte is astonyed, & moued out of hys place.
Heare then the sounde of hys voyce, & the noyse that goeth out of hys mouth.
He gouerneth euery thing vnder the heauen, & his lyghte reacheth vnto the ende of the worlde.
A roarynge voyce foloweth hym: for hys gloryous maiestye geueth suche a thondre clappe, that (though a man heare it) yet may he not perceiue it afterward. It geueth an horryble sounde,
when God sendeth oute hys voyce: greate thynges doth he, whiche we can not comprehende.
When he commaundeth the snow, it falleth vpon the earth: As sone as he geueth the rayne a charge, ymmedyatly the showers haue theyr strength, & fall doune.
He sendeth feare vpon euery man that they myght knowe theyr owne worckes.
The beastes crepe into theyr dennes, and take theyr reste.
Oute of the south commeth the tempest, and coulde out of the north.
At the breth of God, the frost commeth, & the waters are shed abroad.
The cloudes do theyr laboure in geuyng moystnes, the cloudes poure doune theyr rayne.
He dystrybuteth also on euerye syde, accordynge as it pleaseth hym to deale oute hys worckes, that they maye do, whatsoeuer he commaundeth them thorowe the whole worlde:
whether it be to punysh anye lande, or to do good vnto them, that seke him.
Herken vnto this (O Iob) stande styl, and considre the wonderous worckes of God.
Art thou of councel wyth God, when he doth these thinges? When he causeth the lighte to come forthe of his cloudes?
Arte thou of hys councell when he spredeth oute the cloudes? Haste thou the perfect knowledge of his wonders?
and howe thy clothes are warme, when the lande is styll thorowe the Southe wynd
Hast thou helped him to spreade oute the heauen, which is to loke vpon, as it were cast of cleare metall?
Teache vs what we shall saye vnto hym, for we are vnmete because of darcknes
Shall it be tolde hym what I saye? Shulde a man speake, or shuld he kepe it backe?
For euerye man seith not the lighte, that he kepeth cleare in the cloudes, which he clenseth when he maketh the wynde to blowe.
Goulde is brought oute of the Northe, but the prayse & honoure of Gods feare commeth from God hym self.
It is not we that can fynde oute the almighty for in power, equyte, and righteousnesse, he is hyer than can be expressed.
Seyng then that euerye body feareth him, why shuld not all wise men also stande in feare of hym.
38: Then spake the Lorde vnto Iob oute of the storme, and sayd:
what is he that hideth his mynde with folysh wordes?
Gyrde vp thy loynes lyke a man, for I wyl question the, se thou geue me a dyrecte aunswere.
Where wast thou, when I layde the foundacyons of the earth? Tel planely yf thou hast vnderstandyng.
Who hath measured it, knoweste thou? Or, who hath spreade the lyne vpon it?
Wherevpon stande the pylers of it? Or who layed the corner stone?
Where wast thou when the mornyng starres praysed me together & all the chyldren of God reioysed triumphantly?
Who shut the sea with dores, when it brake forth as a chyld oute of his mothers wombe?
When I made the cloudes to be a coueryng for it, & swadled it wyth the darcke?
when I gaue it my commaundement, makynge dores & barres for it,
saying: Hytherto shalt thou come, but no forther, & here shalte thou laye doune thy proude & hye waues.
Haste thou geuen the mornyng his charge (as sone as thou wast borne) and shewed the daye sprynge his place,
that it might take holde of the corners of the earthe, & that the vngodlye myght be shaken out?
Theyr tokens & weapons haste thou turned lyke claye & set them vp agayne as the chaunginge of a garment.
Yea thou hast spoyled the vngodly of theyr lyght, & broken the arme of the proude.
Camest thou euer into the grounde of the sea: or haste thou walked in the lowe corners of the depe?
Haue the gates of death ben opened vnto the, or haste thou sene the dore of euerlasting treasure?
Hast thou also perceiued, how broad the earth is? Nowe yf thou haste knowledge of all,
then shewe me where lyght dwelleth, & where darcknes is:
that thou mayest brynge vs vnto theyr quarters, yf thou canste tell the waye to theyr houses.
Knewest thou (when thou wast borne) how olde thou shuldest be?
Wentest thou euer into the threasuryes of the snowe, or haste thou sene the secrete places of the hayle,
whiche I haue prepared agaynst the tyme of trouble, agaynste the tyme of battell and warre?
By what waye is the lyghte parted, and the heate dealte oute vpon the earth?
Who deuydeth the aboundaunce of waters into ryuers, or who maketh a waye for the stormye wether,
that it watereth & moystureth the drye and baren grounde,
to make the grasse growe in places where no body dwelleth, and in the wyldernes where no man remayneth?
Who is the father of rayne? Or who hath begotten the droppes of dewe?
Oute of whose wombe came the yse? Who hath gendred the coldnes of the ayre?
that the waters are as harde as stones, and lye congeled aboue the depe.
Haste thou brought the .vij. starres together? Or art thou able to breake the circle of heauen?
Canst thou brynge forth the mornynge starre or the euenyng starre at conuenyente tyme, & conueye them home agayne?
Knowest thou the course of heauen, that thou mayest set vp the ordynaunce thereof vpon the earth?
Moreouer canst thou lyfte vp thy voyce to the cloudes, that they maye powre doune a greate rayne vpon the?
Canste thou thondre also that they maye go theyr waye, & be obedient vnto the, saying: Lo here are we.
Who geueth sure wysdome or stedfast vnderstandyng?
who numbreth the cloudes in wysdome? who stylleth the vehement waters of heauen?
who turneth the clottes to duste, & then to be clottes agayne?
Hunteste thou the praye from the lyon, or fedest thou hys welpes
lying in theyr dennes, & lurkyng in theyr couches?
who prouydeth meate for the rauen, when his younge ones crye vnto God, and fle aboute for wante of meate?
39: Knowest thou the tyme when the wylde gotes bringe forthe theyr yonge among the stony rockes? Or layest thou wayte when the hyndes vse to fawne?
rekeneste thou the monethes after they engendre, that thou knowest the tyme of theyr bearynge?
or when they lye doune, when they raste theyr younge ones, & when they are delyuered of theyr trauayle and payne?
How theyr younge ones growe vp & waxe greate thorowe good fedynge?
who letteth the wylde asse go fre, or who louseth the bondes of the mule?
Vnto whom I haue geuen the wyldernes to be their house, & the vntylled lande to be theyr dwellynge place.
That they maye geue no force for the multytude of people in the cytyes, neither regard the crying of the dryuer,
but seke their pasture aboute the mountaynes, and folow the grene grasse.
Whyl the vnicorne be so tame as to do the seruyce, or to abyde styl by thy cryb?
Canste thou bynd the yocke about him in thy sorowes, to make him plowe after the in the valleys?
Mayest thou trust him (because he is strong) or committe thy laboure vnto hym?
Mayest thou beleue him, that he wyll brynge home the corne, or to cary any thyng vnto the barne?
The Estrych (whose fethers are fayrer then the wynges of the sparowe hauke)
when he hath layed hys egges vpon the ground he bredeth them in the dust,
& forgetteth them: so that they myght be troden with fete, or broken with some wylde beaste.
So harde is he vnto hys yong ones, as thoughe they were not hys, & laboureth in vayne wythout anye feare.
And that because God hath taken wysdome from hym, & hath not geuen hym vnderstandynge.
When hys tyme is, he flyeth vp on hye, & careth neyther for horse nor man.
Haste thou geuen the horse his strength, or learned him to bowe doune his necke wt feare:
that he letteth him selfe be dryuen forthe lyke a greshopper, where as the stoute neyenge that he maketh, is fearfull?
he breaketh the grounde with the hoffes of hys fete chearfullye in hys strength, & runneth to mete the harueste men.
He layeth a syde all feare, hys stomack is not abated, neyther starteth he a backe for anye swerde.
Thoughe the quyuers rattle vpon him though the speare & shyld glystre:
yet rusheth he in fearsely, and beateth vpon the grounde, He feareth not the noyse of the trompettes,
but as sone as he heareth the shawmes blow, thushe (sayth he) for he smelleth the battell a farre of, the noyse, the Captaynes and the shoutynge.
Commeth it thorow thy wisdome, that the Goshauke flyeth towarde the South?
Dothe the Aegle mounte vp, and make his neste on hye at the commaundement?
He abydeth in the stonye rockes, and vpon the hye toppes of harde mountaynes, where no man can come.
From thence maye he beholde his praye, and loke farre aboute wyth hys eyes.
His younge ones are fed with bloude, & where any deade bodye lyeth, there is he immediatly.
40: Moreouer, God spake vnto Iob & sayde:
Can he that stryueth with the almightye, be at reste? Shulde not he whiche disputeth with God, geue hym an aunswere?
Iob answered the Lorde, sayinge:
Beholde, I am to vyle a personne, to aunswere the, therfore wyll I laye my hand vpon my mouth.
Ones or twise haue I spoken, but I wyll saye no more.
Then spake the Lorde vnto Iob oute of the storme, & sayd:
Gyrd vp thy loynes lyke a man, & tell me the thynges that I wyl aske the.
Wilt thou disanulle my iudgemente? Or wilt thou condempne me, that thou thy selfe mayest be made righteous?
Is thyne arme then lyke the arme of God? Maketh thy voyce such a sound as hys doeth?
Then arme thy selfe with thyne owne power, vp, decke the in thy ioly araye,
poure oute the indignacyon of thy wrath: se that thou caste doune all the proude,
loke well, that thou makest all suche as be stubborne, to obeye: treade all the vngodlye vnder thy fete,
caste them doune vnto the myre. and couer theyr faces wt darckenesse.
Then wil I confesse also, that thyne owne ryghte hande hath saued the.
Behold Behemoth (whom I made with the) which eateth haye as an oxe:
lo, how strong he is in his loynes, & what power he hathe in the nauell of hys bodye.
He spredeth oute hys tayle like a Cedre tre, all hys vaynes are stife.
His shynnes are lyke pypes of brasse, hys rygge bones are lyke staues of yron.
Fyrste when God made hym, he ordened the wyldernesse for hym,
that the mountaynes shuld geue hym grasse, where all the beastes of the fylde take theyr pastyme.
He lyeth amonge the redes in the Mosses, the fennes
hyde him wyth theyr shadowe, & the wylowes of the broke couer hym rounde about.
Lo, withoute any labour myght he drincke out of the whole floud & suppe of Iordane wythoute anye trayle.
Who darre laye hande vpon him openlye, & vndertake to catche hym? Or, who darre put a hooke thorowe hys nose, & laye a snare for hym.
41: Darrest thou drawe out Leuyathan wt an angle, or bynde hys tonge with a snare?
Canste thou put a rynge in the nose of hym, or bore hys chaftes thorow wt a naule.
Wil he make many fayre wordes wyth the (thinckest thou) or flattre the?
Wyll he make a couenaunt wyth the? Or art thou able for to compel him to do the contynuall seruyce?
Wylt thou take thy pastyme wyth hym as with a byrd, or geue him vnto thy maydens,
that thy companyons maye hewe hym in peces, to be parted amonge the marchaunt men?
Canste thou fyl the net with his skinne, or the fyshe pannyer with hys heade?
Darrest thou laye hande vpon him? It is better for the to consydre what harme might happen the there thorow & not to touche hym.
For when thou thinkest to haue hold vpon hym, he shall begyle the: Euery man also that seyth hym, shal go backe. And why?
there darre none be so bolde as to rayse hym vp. Who is able to stande before me?
Or, who hath geuen me anye thynge afore hande, that I am bound to reward hym againe? All thynges vnder heauen are myne.
I feare hym not, whether he threaten or speake fayre.
Who lyfteth hym vp, & strypeth hym out of hys clothes, or who taketh him by the byt of hys brydle?
Who openeth the dore of hys face? for he hath horryble tethe rounde aboute.
Hys body is couered with scales as it were wyth shyldes, lockt in, kepte, & wel compacte together.
One is so ioyned to another, that no ayre can come in
Yea one hangeth so vpon another, & stycketh so together, that they can not be sundered.
His nesynge is lyke a glysteryng fyre, & his eyes lyke the morning shyne.
Oute of hys mouthe go torches & fyre brandes
oute of hys nostrels there goeth a smoke, like as oute of an hote sethinge pot.
His breth maketh the cotes burne, the flamme goeth out of hys mouth.
In his necke remayneth strength & before hys face sorow is turned to gladnes.
The membres of his body are ioyned so strait one to another, and cleue so fast together, that he can not be moued.
His hert is as herde as a stone, & as faste as the stithye that the hammer man smyteth vpon.
When he goeth, the myghtiest of al are afrayed, & the waues heauy.
If he drawe out the swearde, there maye neyther speare nor brest plate, abyde hym
He setteth as much by a strawe as by yron, and as muche by a rotten stocke as by metall.
He starteth not away for hym that bendeth the bowe: & as for slynge stones, he careth as muche for stubble as for them.
He counteth the hammer no better then a strawe, he laugheth hym to scorne that shaketh the speare.
He treadeth the golde in the myre lyke the sharpe potsherdes.
He maketh the depe to seethe and boyle lyke a pot, & stereth the sea together lyke an oyntment.
The waye is lyght after hym, the depe is hys walkynge place.
Vpon earth is there no power lyke vnto hys, for he is so made that he feareth not.
If a man wyll consydre all hye thinges, thys same is a kynge ouer all the chyldren of pryde.
42: Then Iob aunswered the Lorde, and sayd:
I know that thou hast power ouer all thynges, & that there is no thought hyd vnto the.
For who can kepe his owne councell so secrete, but it shalbe knowne? Therfore haue I spoken vnwysely, seyng these thynges are so hye, & passe myne vnderstandynge.
O herken thou vnto me also, & let me speake: aunswere vnto the thynge that I wyll aske the
I haue geuen dyligente care vnto the, & nowe I se the with mine eyes.
Wherfor I geue myne owne selfe the blame, and take repentaunce in the duste and asshes.

Now when the Lord had spoken these wordes vnto Iob, he sayde vnto Elephas the Themanite: I am displeased with the & thy two frendes, for ye haue not spoken the thyng that is right before me, lyke as my seruaunte Iob hath done.

Therfore take .vij. oxen & .vij. rammes, and go to my seruaunte Iob: offre vp also for your selues a brentofferynge: & let my seruaunte Iob praye for you. Hym wyll I accepte, & not deale with you after youre folishnesse: in that ye haue not spoken the thynge whiche is right, like as my seruaunt Iob hath done.
So Elephas the Themanite, Baldad the Suhyte & Sophar the Naamathite went their waye, and dyd accordynge as the Lorde commaunded them. The Lorde also accepted the personne of Iob,
and the Lorde turned hym vnto Iob, when he prayed for his frendes. Yea the Lorde gaue Iob twyse as muche as he had a fore.

And then came there vnto him all hys brethren, all hys sisters, with all them that had bene of hys acquayntaunce afore, & ate bread wyth hym in hys house, wondryng at hym, & comfortyng hym ouer all the trouble, that the Lorde had brought vpon hym. Euery man gaue hym a shepe and a Iewell of golde.
And the Lorde made Iob rycher then he was before: for he had .xiiij.M. shepe .vi.M. camels, a .M. youcke of oxen, & a .M. asshes.
He had chyldren also .vij. sonnes & .iij. doughters.
The fyrste called daye: the seconde Pouerte: the thyrde all plenteousnes.
In all the lande were none found so fayre, as the doughters of Iob, & theyr father gaue them enherytaunce amonge theyr brethren.
After this lyued Iob .xl. yares, so that he sawe his children, & his children children to the fourthe generacyon.
And so he dyed, beynge olde & of a perfecte age.
